cards.q: An autocrine signal acts on which cell?
cards.a: The same cell that secreted it.
options: The same cell that secreted it
A neighboring cell of a different type
A distant cell reached through the blood
A cell across a synaptic cleft
cards.explanation: Autocrine means self directed, so the molecule binds receptors on the very cell that released it, which is how a cell reinforces or limits its own activity. A neighboring cell of a different type is the paracrine target. A distant cell reached through the blood defines a hormone, and a cell across a synaptic cleft is the target of a neurotransmitter.

cards.q: How does a paracrine signal reach its target?
cards.a: By diffusing a short distance through the interstitial fluid.
options: By traveling in the blood to distant tissues
By diffusing a short distance through the interstitial fluid
By moving through gap junctions into the next cell
By crossing a synaptic cleft from an axon terminal
cards.explanation: A paracrine is secreted into the interstitial fluid and diffuses only as far as neighboring cells, which limits its range to roughly the local tissue. Travel in the blood is the hormone route. Movement through gap junctions is direct coupling rather than secretion into extracellular fluid, and crossing a synaptic cleft is what a neurotransmitter does.

cards.q: Where is a neurotransmitter released?
cards.a: From an axon terminal into a synaptic cleft.
options: From an endocrine cell into a capillary
From a neuron ending into the bloodstream
From an axon terminal into a synaptic cleft
From any cell into the surrounding interstitial fluid
cards.explanation: A neurotransmitter is released from an axon terminal into the narrow synaptic cleft, so it crosses well under a micrometer and acts on one identified target cell. Release from an endocrine cell into a capillary describes a hormone. Release from a neuron ending into the bloodstream describes a neurohormone, and nonspecific release into interstitial fluid describes a paracrine.

cards.q: What makes a molecule a neurohormone rather than a neurotransmitter?
cards.a: A neuron secretes it into the blood instead of into a synapse.
options: It is made from an amino acid rather than from cholesterol
It is released by an endocrine gland rather than by a neuron
It binds an intracellular receptor rather than a surface receptor
A neuron secretes it into the blood instead of into a synapse
cards.explanation: Both are made and released by neurons, so the distinguishing feature is the delivery route: a neurohormone enters the bloodstream and reaches distant targets, while a neurotransmitter stays in the synapse. Chemical family does not decide the class, since the same molecule can serve as either. Receptor location is a separate property, and release by an endocrine gland would make the molecule a classical hormone.

cards.q: A classical hormone is secreted by which kind of cell and carried by what?
cards.a: By an endocrine cell, carried in the blood.
options: By an endocrine cell, carried in the blood
By a neuron, carried across a synapse
By an epithelial cell, carried in interstitial fluid
By an immune cell, carried through gap junctions
cards.explanation: A hormone is defined by an endocrine cell releasing it into the blood, which is why every tissue is exposed to it and only cells with the receptor respond. A neuron releasing across a synapse is a neurotransmitter. Release into interstitial fluid without entering blood is paracrine, and gap junction transfer is not hormonal secretion at all.

cards.q: Which two signal classes use the bloodstream as their route of travel?
cards.a: Hormones and neurohormones.
options: Hormones and paracrines
Hormones and neurohormones
Neurotransmitters and paracrines
Autocrines and neurotransmitters
cards.explanation: Hormones come from endocrine cells and neurohormones come from neurons, but both are released into the blood and can act on distant targets. Paracrines and autocrines stay in the local interstitial fluid and never depend on circulation. Neurotransmitters remain inside the synaptic cleft, which is why their effect is restricted to one postsynaptic cell.

cards.q: Every cell in the body is exposed to a circulating hormone. What determines which cells actually respond?
cards.a: Whether the cell expresses a receptor for that hormone.
options: Whether the cell is electrically excitable
How close the cell is to the gland that made it
Whether the cell expresses a receptor for that hormone
How much blood flow the tissue receives
cards.explanation: Specificity in the endocrine system comes from the receptor, not from delivery, so a cell without the matching receptor sits in the same plasma concentration and does nothing. Distance from the gland does not matter once the molecule is in the general circulation. Excitability governs action potentials, not hormone binding, and blood flow changes how fast a hormone arrives but not whether the cell can read it.

cards.q: Which class of chemical signal produces the fastest onset of response, on the order of milliseconds?
cards.a: Neurotransmitter.
options: Hormone
Neurohormone
Paracrine
Neurotransmitter
cards.explanation: A neurotransmitter travels a fraction of a micrometer to a receptor already waiting on the postsynaptic membrane, so onset is measured in milliseconds. Hormones and neurohormones must be carried by the circulation, which takes seconds to minutes at best. Paracrines are faster than hormones because the diffusion distance is short, but they still take longer than synaptic transmission and spread more diffusely.

cards.q: A mast cell in the skin releases histamine, which binds receptors on capillary endothelial cells a few micrometers away. How is histamine acting here?
cards.a: As a paracrine.
options: As a paracrine
As an autocrine
As a neurohormone
As a hormone
cards.explanation: The signal is secreted into interstitial fluid and acts on nearby cells of a different type without entering the blood, which is the definition of paracrine action. Autocrine would require histamine to act back on the mast cell itself, which also happens but is not what is described here. It is not a hormone because it is not carried by blood to distant targets, and it is not a neurohormone because a mast cell is not a neuron.

cards.q: An activated T cell secretes interleukin 2, which binds interleukin 2 receptors on that same T cell and drives it to divide. Classify this signal.
cards.a: Autocrine.
options: Paracrine
Autocrine
Hormone
Neurotransmitter
cards.explanation: The secreting cell is also the responding cell, so this is autocrine, and it creates a positive feedback loop that expands the clone. It would be paracrine only if the responding cells were neighbors rather than the secretor itself. It is not a hormone because no blood transport is involved, and it is not a neurotransmitter because there is no neuron and no synapse.

cards.q: A sympathetic neuron releases norepinephrine into a narrow gap where it binds beta 1 receptors on cardiac cells. Classify norepinephrine in this situation.
cards.a: Neurotransmitter.
options: Neurohormone
Paracrine
Neurotransmitter
Hormone
cards.explanation: A neuron is releasing the molecule directly onto an identified target across a synapse, so it is functioning as a neurotransmitter. The same molecule counts as a neurohormone only when a neuron releases it into blood. Paracrine would require release into general interstitial fluid rather than a synapse, and hormone would require an endocrine cell and blood transport.

cards.q: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are modified sympathetic neurons that release epinephrine straight into the blood. Epinephrine released this way is best classified as which of the following?
cards.a: A neurohormone.
options: A neurotransmitter
A paracrine
An autocrine
A neurohormone
cards.explanation: The releasing cell is neural in origin and the molecule enters the circulation to reach distant targets, and that combination defines a neurohormone. Calling it a neurotransmitter would require a synapse and a single postsynaptic cell. Paracrine and autocrine both require the molecule to stay in local interstitial fluid rather than being carried away by blood.

cards.q: Beta cells of the pancreas release insulin into pancreatic capillaries, and insulin then acts on muscle, liver, and fat throughout the body. Classify insulin.
cards.a: A hormone.
options: A hormone
A neurohormone
A paracrine
An autocrine
cards.explanation: An endocrine cell secretes it into blood and it acts on many distant tissues, which is the classical hormone pattern. It is not a neurohormone because a beta cell is an endocrine cell, not a neuron. It is not paracrine or autocrine in this description, although insulin does also act locally on neighboring islet cells, which shows one molecule can occupy more than one class depending on route.

cards.q: Endothelial cells lining an arteriole make nitric oxide, which diffuses into the smooth muscle immediately beneath them and relaxes it. Nitric oxide here is acting as which class of signal?
cards.a: A paracrine.
options: A hormone
A paracrine
A neurotransmitter
An autocrine
cards.explanation: The molecule moves a few cell diameters through tissue to a different nearby cell type, which is paracrine signaling, and its very short half life keeps the effect local. It cannot act as a hormone because it is destroyed long before the circulation could distribute it. It is not autocrine because the responding cell is the smooth muscle, not the endothelial cell, and no neuron or synapse is involved.

cards.q: Norepinephrine can be called a neurotransmitter in one setting and a neurohormone in another. What decides which label applies?
cards.a: The route the molecule takes to its target.
options: The chemical structure of the molecule
The type of receptor the molecule binds
The route the molecule takes to its target
The speed at which the molecule is degraded
cards.explanation: These classes are defined by delivery, so release into a synapse makes it a neurotransmitter and release into blood makes it a neurohormone, with the molecule unchanged. Structure cannot decide it, because the structure is identical in both cases. Receptor type varies by target tissue rather than by class, and degradation rate affects duration of action, not classification.

cards.q: A paracrine molecule is normally destroyed within seconds by an enzyme in the interstitial fluid. A drug inhibits that enzyme. Predict the effect on the molecule's range and on the number of cells it reaches.
cards.a: Range increases and more cells respond, because the molecule survives long enough to diffuse farther.
options: Range increases but fewer cells respond, because the diluted molecule falls below threshold everywhere
Range decreases and fewer cells respond, because degradation normally pushes the molecule outward
Range is unchanged but each target cell responds more strongly, because diffusion distance is fixed
Range increases and more cells respond, because the molecule survives long enough to diffuse farther
cards.explanation: Diffusion distance is set by how long a molecule survives, so blocking its breakdown lets it spread over a wider radius and recruit target cells that were previously out of reach. Degradation restricts spread rather than promoting it, so any answer claiming that breakdown pushes the molecule outward reverses the logic. Saying the range is unchanged is wrong because the affected volume is exactly what changes, and predicting fewer responding cells is wrong because concentration near the source stays high and above threshold even as the field widens.

cards.q: A stressful stimulus triggers both sympathetic nerve firing to the heart and adrenal release of epinephrine into the blood. Which statement correctly describes onset and duration of the two responses?
cards.a: The neural effect starts first and ends quickly, and the blood borne effect starts later and lasts longer.
options: The neural effect starts first and ends quickly, and the blood borne effect starts later and lasts longer
The blood borne effect starts first, because blood moves faster than an action potential
Both start together, but the neural effect lasts longer because axons keep firing
The neural effect starts first and lasts longer, and the blood borne effect is brief because plasma dilutes it
cards.explanation: Synaptic delivery covers a fraction of a micrometer and the transmitter is cleared in milliseconds, so the neural response is immediate and short. Circulating epinephrine needs seconds to reach the heart and is cleared over minutes, so it comes on later and outlasts the neural signal. Blood transport is far slower than synaptic transmission, and dilution in plasma lowers peak concentration without shortening exposure time.

cards.q: In an isolated tissue preparation, a signal keeps affecting cells inside the tissue after perfusion is stopped, but a target organ downstream loses its response. What does this tell you about the signal?
cards.a: It acts locally as a paracrine within the tissue and as a blood borne signal on the distant organ.
options: It acts only as a hormone, since stopping perfusion abolished the response in the distant target organ
It acts locally as a paracrine within the tissue and as a blood borne signal on the distant organ
It must be a neurotransmitter, since the local effect survived loss of perfusion
It is an autocrine, since only the tissue that made it still responded
cards.explanation: The surviving local effect shows that diffusion through interstitial fluid is enough there, while the lost distant effect shows the far target depended on circulatory delivery, so the molecule fills both roles. It cannot be only a hormone, because a pure hormone effect would vanish everywhere once transport stopped. Nothing in the setup involves a synapse, and the local response includes cells other than the secretor, which rules out a strictly autocrine reading.

cards.q: Intravenous epinephrine changes heart rate, airway diameter, and liver glucose output at once, while stimulating the sympathetic nerve to the heart changes only heart rate. What accounts for the difference?
cards.a: The blood delivers the molecule to every tissue that has the receptor, while a nerve delivers it to one target.
options: Intravenous epinephrine binds a different receptor than neurally released norepinephrine
Intravenous epinephrine is more potent per molecule than a transmitter released from a nerve terminal at a synapse
The blood delivers the molecule to every tissue that has the receptor, while a nerve delivers it to one target
Nerve stimulation activates only intracellular receptors, so its effects cannot spread
cards.explanation: Route determines breadth of effect, so circulating molecules reach all receptor bearing tissues while synaptic release confines the signal to the innervated cell. Receptor identity is not the deciding factor, since adrenergic receptors in these tissues respond to both molecules. Potency per molecule does not create a multiorgan pattern, and neurally released transmitters bind surface receptors just as circulating ones do.

cards.q: A lipid soluble signal molecule most often binds a receptor located where?
cards.a: Inside the cell, in the cytosol or nucleus.
options: On the outer face of the plasma membrane
Bound to the outside of a plasma protein in blood
In the extracellular matrix outside the cell
Inside the cell, in the cytosol or nucleus
cards.explanation: Being lipid soluble lets the molecule pass straight through the phospholipid bilayer, so its receptor can sit in the cytosol or nucleus where the complex can act on DNA. A receptor on the outer membrane face is what a water soluble signal needs, since that signal cannot cross. Receptors are not free in the matrix, and plasma binding proteins carry hormones in blood but do not transmit a signal.

cards.q: Peptide hormones such as insulin bind receptors in what location?
cards.a: On the plasma membrane surface.
options: On the plasma membrane surface
In the nucleus, bound to DNA
Free in the cytosol
On the inner mitochondrial membrane
cards.explanation: Peptides are polar and often charged, so they cannot cross the hydrophobic core of the membrane and must signal through a receptor whose binding site faces the extracellular fluid. Nuclear and cytosolic receptors are used by steroid and thyroid hormones, which do cross. Mitochondrial membranes are not an entry point for peptide hormone signaling.

cards.q: Why do steroid hormones travel in blood bound to carrier proteins?
cards.a: Because they are poorly soluble in the watery plasma.
options: Because carrier binding is required for receptor activation
Because they are poorly soluble in the watery plasma
Because carriers speed their movement across capillary walls
Because carriers convert them into their active form
cards.explanation: A lipophilic molecule dissolves badly in plasma, so a carrier protein keeps it in solution and creates a circulating reservoir. Only the free fraction can enter cells and bind receptors, so carrier binding is the opposite of a requirement for activation. Carriers slow rather than speed movement out of the capillary, and conversion to a more potent form happens by enzymes in target tissues, not by the carrier.

cards.q: Once a steroid hormone binds its intracellular receptor, what does the hormone receptor complex do?
cards.a: Binds DNA and changes the transcription of specific genes.
options: Opens an ion channel in the nuclear envelope
Phosphorylates proteins already present in the cytosol
Binds DNA and changes the transcription of specific genes
Activates adenylyl cyclase to raise cyclic AMP
cards.explanation: The activated complex works as a transcription factor, binding regulatory DNA sequences and turning synthesis of particular proteins up or down. Opening ion channels and activating adenylyl cyclase are membrane receptor mechanisms that use second messengers. Direct phosphorylation of existing proteins describes kinase driven pathways, which act far faster and need no new gene products.

cards.q: Which receptor type generally produces the faster cellular response?
cards.a: A membrane surface receptor.
options: A receptor already bound to a DNA response element
A cytosolic steroid receptor
A nuclear thyroid hormone receptor
A membrane surface receptor
cards.explanation: Surface receptors modify proteins that already exist, usually by phosphorylation or by opening channels, so effects appear within seconds. Cytosolic and nuclear receptors both work by changing gene transcription, which requires transcription, translation, and protein accumulation, so they take tens of minutes to hours. A receptor sitting on a response element is a nuclear receptor and shares that same slow time course.

cards.q: Thyroid hormone is made from an amino acid but still binds a nuclear receptor. What property allows that?
cards.a: It is lipophilic enough to cross the plasma membrane.
options: It is lipophilic enough to cross the plasma membrane
It is small enough to fit through membrane pores
It is carried into the nucleus by a G protein
It is charged and therefore attracted to nuclear DNA
cards.explanation: Chemical family predicts receptor location only loosely, and thyroid hormone is the exception because solubility, not amino acid origin, decides where the receptor sits. Membrane pores do not admit hormone sized molecules by simple sieving. G proteins work on the cytosolic side of surface receptors and do not carry cargo into the nucleus, and a charged molecule would be trapped outside the cell rather than drawn to DNA.

cards.q: Catecholamines such as epinephrine are water soluble. Where do their receptors sit?
cards.a: On the plasma membrane.
options: In the nucleus
On the plasma membrane
In the cytosol
In the endoplasmic reticulum lumen
cards.explanation: Water soluble signals cannot cross the lipid bilayer, so their receptors face the extracellular fluid and the message is relayed inward by second messengers. Nuclear and cytosolic receptors serve hormones that can enter the cell on their own. The endoplasmic reticulum lumen holds the calcium store used later in some of these pathways, but it is not where epinephrine binds.

cards.q: What physically stops a peptide hormone from entering a cell by simple diffusion?
cards.a: The hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer.
options: The negative charge of the cytosol
The thickness of the extracellular matrix
The hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer
The tight junctions between neighboring cells
cards.explanation: The fatty acid core of the membrane is a nonpolar barrier, and a polar, hydrogen bonding peptide cannot shed its water shell to cross it. The negative resting potential of the cytosol affects ion movement, not a large uncharged peptide. The matrix is porous to hormone sized molecules, and tight junctions block movement between cells rather than into one cell.

cards.q: A newly isolated signal molecule is highly lipid soluble. Predict where its receptor is and how fast its effects appear.
cards.a: Intracellular receptor, with effects appearing over tens of minutes to hours.
options: Surface receptor, with effects appearing within a few seconds
Intracellular receptor, with effects appearing within milliseconds
Surface receptor, with effects delayed by many hours after binding
Intracellular receptor, with effects appearing over tens of minutes to hours
cards.explanation: Lipid solubility means the molecule crosses the membrane and finds a receptor that works through gene transcription, and making new protein takes tens of minutes to hours. A surface receptor with fast effects is the prediction for a water soluble signal. Pairing a surface receptor with an hour long delay, or an intracellular receptor with millisecond onset, mismatches the mechanism with its time course.

cards.q: A hormone changes the activity of an existing enzyme within 10 seconds of exposure. Which receptor type is it most likely using?
cards.a: A surface receptor.
options: A surface receptor
A cytosolic steroid receptor
A nuclear thyroid hormone receptor
A DNA binding receptor in the nucleus
cards.explanation: Ten seconds is far too short for transcription and translation, so the hormone must be modifying proteins that are already present, which is the signature of surface receptor signaling. The other three are all transcription linked receptors whose effects require new protein and cannot appear that fast. Those receptors would instead explain a response measured in hours.

cards.q: A drug that blocks RNA polymerase abolishes a hormone's effect on a target cell. What does that tell you about the receptor?
cards.a: It is an intracellular receptor working through gene transcription.
options: It is a surface receptor coupled to a G protein and a second messenger
It is an intracellular receptor working through gene transcription
It is a ligand gated ion channel
It is a surface receptor with kinase activity
cards.explanation: If stopping transcription stops the response, the response depends on new messenger RNA, and that is the mechanism of a cytosolic or nuclear receptor. G protein pathways, ion channels, and receptor kinases all act on proteins that already exist, so their immediate effects survive a transcription blocker. Those pathways can change gene expression eventually, but their fast effects would remain.

cards.q: Two hormones are infused at the same rate. The water soluble one has a plasma half life of about 5 minutes and the lipid soluble one about 90 minutes. What best explains the difference?
cards.a: The lipid soluble hormone circulates bound to carrier proteins, which shields it from filtration.
options: The lipid soluble hormone binds more receptors, which slows its clearance from plasma
The water soluble hormone is destroyed by stomach acid before it reaches the blood
The lipid soluble hormone circulates bound to carrier proteins, which shields it from filtration
The water soluble hormone diffuses into cells faster, removing it from the plasma
cards.explanation: Carrier bound hormone is not free to be filtered at the kidney or attacked by plasma enzymes, so the bound reservoir slowly resupplies the free fraction and stretches the half life. Stomach acid is irrelevant to an infused hormone that never enters the digestive tract. Receptor binding removes only a tiny fraction of circulating hormone, and a water soluble hormone cannot diffuse into cells at all.

cards.q: A pharmacologist wants a molecule that can be swallowed, cross membranes freely, and act on a nuclear receptor. Which property must the molecule have?
cards.a: High lipid solubility.
options: A large positive charge
A permanent covalent bond to a carrier protein
A long chain of polar amino acids
High lipid solubility
cards.explanation: Only a lipophilic molecule can slip through the bilayer of intestinal cells and then of target cells to reach a nuclear receptor. Strong charge and polar peptide chains both trap the molecule in water, which is exactly why peptide hormones must be injected and must use surface receptors. A permanent bond to a carrier would prevent the free molecule from ever entering a cell.

cards.q: After a hormone is washed out of the bath, a cultured cell keeps showing increased activity of one enzyme for the next 12 hours. Which receptor mechanism best explains the persistence?
cards.a: An intracellular receptor that increased synthesis of the enzyme protein.
options: An intracellular receptor that increased synthesis of the enzyme protein
A ligand gated ion channel that stayed open
A G protein coupled receptor with cyclic AMP still bound to protein kinase A
A surface receptor whose ligand cannot be washed off
cards.explanation: Persistence long after the ligand is gone points to new protein molecules that remain in the cell until they are degraded, which is what transcription linked receptors produce. Ion channels close within milliseconds of ligand removal. Cyclic AMP is broken down by phosphodiesterase within seconds to minutes, and a ligand that cannot be washed off would be an unusual covalent case rather than the ordinary explanation.

cards.q: Which combination of solubility, receptor location, and duration is internally consistent?
cards.a: Lipophilic, intracellular receptor, long lasting response.
options: Hydrophilic, intracellular receptor, long lasting response
Lipophilic, intracellular receptor, long lasting response
Lipophilic, surface receptor, brief response
Hydrophilic, surface receptor, long response driven by new protein synthesis
cards.explanation: Lipid solubility permits entry, an intracellular receptor changes transcription, and the resulting proteins persist, so all three parts fit together. A hydrophilic molecule cannot reach an intracellular receptor at all. A lipophilic molecule using a surface receptor contradicts the reason its receptor is inside, and the standard hydrophilic pattern is a fast, brief response from modifying proteins that already exist.

cards.q: Cells are pretreated with a protein synthesis inhibitor, then exposed to epinephrine and to cortisol. Predict the result for each.
cards.a: The epinephrine response persists and the cortisol response is lost.
options: Both responses are lost
The cortisol response persists and the epinephrine response is lost
The epinephrine response persists and the cortisol response is lost
Both responses persist unchanged
cards.explanation: Epinephrine works through a surface receptor and second messengers that modify enzymes already present, so it does not need the ribosome. Cortisol works through an intracellular receptor whose entire output is new protein, so blocking translation removes its effect. Reversing the two swaps the mechanisms, and saying both survive ignores cortisol's dependence on gene expression.

cards.q: A lipophilic hormone is injected. Nothing measurable happens for about an hour, then the effect builds and lasts most of a day. Which two features of the mechanism explain the delay and the duration?
cards.a: Transcription and translation take time, and the newly made proteins persist until they are degraded.
options: The hormone must be converted to a water soluble form first, then it is slowly cleared
Second messenger levels rise slowly, and phosphodiesterase is unusually slow in this cell
The hormone must saturate its carrier protein first, then receptors slowly recycle
Transcription and translation take time, and the newly made proteins persist until they are degraded
cards.explanation: The lag matches the time needed to transcribe messenger RNA and translate protein, and the long tail matches the lifetime of those protein molecules once they exist. Conversion to a water soluble form is not required for action and would in fact block cell entry. Carrier saturation shifts free hormone levels without creating an hour long lag, and second messengers are not part of a nuclear receptor pathway.

cards.q: A peptide is chemically modified by attaching a long fatty acid chain, which makes it strongly lipophilic. Predict two consequences for its signaling.
cards.a: It can now reach intracellular targets, and it will need a carrier to stay dissolved in plasma.
options: It can now reach intracellular targets, and it will need a carrier to stay dissolved in plasma
It will act faster, because lipophilic molecules activate surface receptors more efficiently
It will lose all activity, because only unmodified peptides can bind any receptor
It will act only outside the cell, because added lipid always blocks the binding site
cards.explanation: Adding lipid character changes both halves of the story: membrane crossing becomes possible, and plasma solubility becomes a problem that carrier proteins solve. Lipophilicity does not make surface receptor activation more efficient, and gene mediated effects are slower rather than faster. A modified peptide can still be recognized by a binding site, and a fatty acid tail does not automatically occlude it.

cards.q: A person has a low plasma concentration of cortisol binding globulin. Total plasma cortisol measures low, free cortisol is normal, and the tissues behave normally. Why?
cards.a: Only free hormone can enter cells, so tissue signaling tracks the free fraction rather than the total.
options: Carrier bound hormone is the active pool, so the tissues are actually mildly underexposed
Only free hormone can enter cells, so tissue signaling tracks the free fraction rather than the total
Low carrier levels force the adrenal gland to make a more potent form of cortisol
Cortisol switches to a surface receptor when carrier levels fall, which preserves the response
cards.explanation: The bound fraction is a reservoir, not the signal, so a smaller reservoir lowers the total measurement while normal feedback keeps the free level where it belongs. Treating bound hormone as the active pool inverts the relationship. The adrenal gland does not synthesize a different molecule in response to carrier levels, and receptor location follows the hormone's solubility and does not switch.

cards.q: Which nucleotide is bound to the alpha subunit of a G protein when the G protein is inactive?
cards.a: GDP.
options: ATP
GTP
GDP
Cyclic AMP
cards.explanation: The resting G protein holds GDP on its alpha subunit, and activation is the exchange of that GDP for GTP after the receptor binds ligand. GTP marks the active state, so it is the answer to the opposite question. ATP is the substrate adenylyl cyclase uses, and cyclic AMP is the product further down the pathway, neither of which sits on the G protein.

cards.q: What happens on the G protein alpha subunit immediately after a ligand binds its G protein coupled receptor?
cards.a: GDP is released and GTP binds in its place.
options: GTP is hydrolyzed to GDP
The subunit binds cyclic AMP
The subunit is phosphorylated by protein kinase A
GDP is released and GTP binds in its place
cards.explanation: The activated receptor acts as an exchange factor, prying GDP off so the more abundant GTP can bind, and the GTP bound alpha subunit is what activates the amplifier enzyme. Hydrolysis of GTP back to GDP is the later step that shuts the pathway off. Protein kinase A acts far downstream on target proteins, and cyclic AMP binds protein kinase A, not the G protein.

cards.q: Which amplifier enzyme does an activated Gs protein turn on?
cards.a: Adenylyl cyclase.
options: Adenylyl cyclase
Phospholipase C
Protein kinase A
Phosphodiesterase
cards.explanation: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase in the membrane, which is the amplifier step that converts one activated G protein into many second messenger molecules. Phospholipase C is the amplifier enzyme for Gq instead. Protein kinase A is the target of the second messenger rather than its maker, and phosphodiesterase destroys cyclic AMP, so activating it would end the signal.

cards.q: Adenylyl cyclase converts which substrate into cyclic AMP?
cards.a: ATP.
options: GTP
ATP
ADP
PIP2
cards.explanation: Adenylyl cyclase takes ATP and cyclizes it into cyclic AMP, which is why a cell with plentiful ATP can make second messenger quickly. GTP is the nucleotide that activates the G protein itself, a different step. ADP is not the substrate, and PIP2 is the membrane lipid that phospholipase C splits in the Gq pathway.

cards.q: Cyclic AMP produces most of its effects by activating which protein?
cards.a: Protein kinase A.
options: Adenylyl cyclase
Protein kinase C
Protein kinase A
Phospholipase C
cards.explanation: Cyclic AMP binds the regulatory subunits of protein kinase A, freeing the catalytic subunits to phosphorylate target proteins and change their activity. Protein kinase C is activated by diacylglycerol and calcium in the Gq pathway. Adenylyl cyclase makes cyclic AMP rather than responding to it, and phospholipase C belongs to the other branch entirely.

cards.q: Which amplifier enzyme is activated by a Gq protein?
cards.a: Phospholipase C.
options: Adenylyl cyclase
Guanylyl cyclase
Protein kinase A
Phospholipase C
cards.explanation: Gq activates phospholipase C, which cleaves the membrane lipid PIP2 into IP3 and diacylglycerol. Adenylyl cyclase is the Gs amplifier. Guanylyl cyclase makes cyclic GMP and is typically activated by nitric oxide or by a receptor enzyme rather than by Gq, and protein kinase A is a downstream target, not an amplifier.

cards.q: Phospholipase C splits PIP2 into which two products?
cards.a: IP3 and diacylglycerol.
options: IP3 and diacylglycerol
ATP and cyclic GMP
Cyclic AMP and pyrophosphate
Calcium and calmodulin
cards.explanation: One membrane lipid yields two second messengers at once, the water soluble IP3 that diffuses into the cytosol and the lipid soluble diacylglycerol that stays in the membrane. Cyclic AMP comes from ATP by way of adenylyl cyclase, a separate pathway. Cyclic GMP comes from GTP by way of guanylyl cyclase, and calcium and calmodulin are downstream participants rather than cleavage products.

cards.q: What does an activated Gi protein do to adenylyl cyclase?
cards.a: Inhibits it, so less cyclic AMP is made.
options: Stimulates it, so more cyclic AMP is made
Inhibits it, so less cyclic AMP is made
Converts it into phospholipase C
Has no effect on it, since Gi acts only on ion channels
cards.explanation: The i in Gi stands for inhibitory, and its alpha subunit lowers adenylyl cyclase activity so cyclic AMP falls below its resting level. Stimulation is the job of Gs. Enzymes are not converted from one to another by G proteins, and although Gi subunits can also open potassium channels, their defining action on this pathway is inhibition of the cyclase.

cards.q: An agonist binds a Gs coupled receptor on a liver cell. Predict what happens to cytosolic cyclic AMP and to protein kinase A activity.
cards.a: Both rise.
options: Cyclic AMP rises and protein kinase A activity falls
Both fall
Both rise
Cyclic AMP falls and protein kinase A activity rises
cards.explanation: Gs turns on adenylyl cyclase, cyclic AMP accumulates, and that cyclic AMP releases the catalytic subunits of protein kinase A, so the two move together. Cyclic AMP does not inhibit protein kinase A, which rules out the split answers. Both falling is the prediction for a Gi coupled agonist instead.

cards.q: A drug locks the G protein alpha subunit in its GTP bound form. Predict the effect on second messenger production.
cards.a: Production continues even after the ligand leaves the receptor.
options: Production stops immediately, because the cycle cannot restart
Production rises only while ligand is present, then stops normally
Production becomes dependent on new receptor synthesis
Production continues even after the ligand leaves the receptor
cards.explanation: The GTP bound alpha subunit is the active form, so preventing its return to the GDP state leaves the amplifier enzyme permanently switched on and independent of ligand. Production cannot stop, because the off step is exactly what has been blocked. New receptor synthesis is irrelevant when the G protein is already active, and normal termination is what the drug prevents.

cards.q: A ligand activates a Gq coupled receptor on vascular smooth muscle. Predict the direction of change in cytosolic calcium.
cards.a: It rises, because IP3 releases calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum.
options: It rises, because IP3 releases calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum
It falls, because IP3 pumps calcium back into stores
It is unchanged, because the Gq pathway acts only on gene transcription
It rises, but only if extracellular calcium is removed first
cards.explanation: IP3 diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum and opens calcium release channels, so cytosolic calcium climbs and can then act as a second messenger of its own. IP3 opens release channels rather than driving the pumps that refill stores. The Gq pathway acts on existing proteins within seconds, and removing extracellular calcium is not required, since the released calcium comes from internal stores.

cards.q: Norepinephrine binds a beta 1 receptor on a cardiac cell and the cell contracts more forcefully. Which sequence matches this pathway?
cards.a: Receptor, Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cyclic AMP, protein kinase A.
options: Receptor, Gq, phospholipase C, IP3, protein kinase C
Receptor, Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cyclic AMP, protein kinase A
Receptor, Gi, adenylyl cyclase, cyclic AMP, protein kinase A
Receptor, Gs, phospholipase C, diacylglycerol, protein kinase A
cards.explanation: Beta receptors couple to Gs, which raises cyclic AMP and activates protein kinase A to phosphorylate calcium channels and contractile regulators. The Gq sequence is the correct chain for alpha 1 receptors, not beta 1. Gi would lower cyclic AMP rather than raise it, and mixing Gs with phospholipase C pairs the wrong G protein with the wrong amplifier enzyme.

cards.q: An agonist activates a Gi coupled receptor. Predict what happens to cyclic AMP in that cell.
cards.a: It falls below the resting level.
options: It rises sharply
It stays constant while IP3 rises
It falls below the resting level
It rises slowly over several hours
cards.explanation: Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, so ongoing production drops while phosphodiesterase keeps degrading what is there, and the net level falls. A sharp rise is the Gs result. IP3 belongs to the Gq branch and is not generated by Gi, and a slow rise over hours describes a transcription driven response, not a second messenger.

cards.q: Adenylyl cyclase is completely inhibited in a cell. A Gs coupled agonist is then applied. Which step still occurs?
cards.a: The G protein alpha subunit still exchanges GDP for GTP.
options: Cyclic AMP still accumulates
Protein kinase A is still activated
Target proteins are still phosphorylated by protein kinase A
The G protein alpha subunit still exchanges GDP for GTP
cards.explanation: The block sits at the amplifier enzyme, so everything upstream of it, including ligand binding and nucleotide exchange on the G protein, proceeds normally. Cyclic AMP cannot accumulate because the enzyme that makes it is disabled. Without cyclic AMP, protein kinase A stays inhibited by its regulatory subunits and no downstream phosphorylation follows.

cards.q: Which ordering correctly describes the flow of information in a G protein coupled receptor pathway?
cards.a: Ligand, receptor, G protein, amplifier enzyme, second messenger, response.
options: Ligand, receptor, G protein, amplifier enzyme, second messenger, response
Ligand, G protein, receptor, second messenger, amplifier enzyme, response
Ligand, receptor, second messenger, G protein, amplifier enzyme, response
Ligand, amplifier enzyme, receptor, G protein, second messenger, response
cards.explanation: The ligand is read by the receptor, the receptor activates the G protein, the G protein switches on the amplifier enzyme, and that enzyme makes the second messenger that produces the response. Putting the G protein ahead of the receptor breaks the coupling that gives these receptors their name. The other two orders place the second messenger or the amplifier enzyme before the enzyme or the receptor that produces them.

cards.q: A bacterial toxin destroys the GTPase activity of the Gs alpha subunit in intestinal cells. Trace the consequence through the pathway.
cards.a: The alpha subunit stays active, adenylyl cyclase keeps running, and cyclic AMP stays high for hours.
options: The alpha subunit can no longer bind GTP at all, so cyclic AMP falls to zero
The alpha subunit stays active, adenylyl cyclase keeps running, and cyclic AMP stays high for hours
Adenylyl cyclase is converted into phospholipase C, so IP3 rises in its place and calcium follows
Cyclic AMP rises briefly and then returns to its baseline right on schedule
cards.explanation: GTPase activity is the built in timer that shuts the alpha subunit off, so removing it leaves the subunit locked in the active conformation and the cyclase producing cyclic AMP long after ligand is gone. GTP binding is untouched by the toxin, so the pathway is stuck on rather than off. No enzyme is converted into another, and the normal return to baseline is precisely what has been lost.

cards.q: Acetylcholine slows the heart through a receptor coupled to Gi but contracts gut smooth muscle through a receptor coupled to Gq. What does this tell you about how the cellular response is determined?
cards.a: The response depends on the receptor subtype and the G protein it couples to, not on the ligand alone.
options: The response depends on the ligand concentration, since higher levels switch the receptor to another G protein
The response depends on how quickly the ligand is degraded in each tissue
The response depends on the receptor subtype and the G protein it couples to, not on the ligand alone
The response depends on whether the ligand is lipid soluble in that tissue
cards.explanation: One molecule can produce opposite effects because each target cell decides the outcome through its receptor subtype, its G protein, and the downstream machinery it happens to express. Concentration changes the size of a response but does not reroute a receptor to a different G protein. Degradation rate alters duration, and the lipid solubility of acetylcholine is a property of the molecule, not of the tissue.

cards.q: In a cell whose membrane PIP2 has been depleted, a Gq agonist is applied. Predict what happens at the receptor, at IP3, and at cytosolic calcium.
cards.a: The receptor and G protein activate normally, but IP3 is not made and calcium does not rise.
options: Calcium rises even higher, because phospholipase C is freed to act on other lipids
Nothing binds the receptor, so no step in the pathway occurs
IP3 is made from ATP instead, so calcium rises normally
The receptor and G protein activate normally, but IP3 is not made and calcium does not rise
cards.explanation: PIP2 is the substrate, not the switch, so ligand binding and G protein activation still happen while the amplifier enzyme has nothing to cleave and generates no messenger. Ligand binding depends on the receptor, which is intact. IP3 comes only from PIP2 and cannot be made from ATP, and with no IP3 there is no signal to open the endoplasmic reticulum calcium channels.

cards.q: An agonist produces no response in a cell, but adding a membrane permeant cyclic AMP analog to the same cell produces the full response. Where is the defect?
cards.a: At or above adenylyl cyclase, since everything downstream of cyclic AMP still works.
options: At or above adenylyl cyclase, since everything downstream of cyclic AMP still works
At protein kinase A, since the kinase is the final common step
At the target proteins, since they can no longer be phosphorylated
At phosphodiesterase, since the cyclic AMP being made is destroyed too quickly to act
cards.explanation: Bypassing the pathway with cyclic AMP itself restores the response, which proves the kinase and all downstream machinery are intact and places the lesion at the receptor, the G protein, or the cyclase. A defect in protein kinase A or in the target proteins would block the analog as well. Excess phosphodiesterase would also degrade the added analog, so the response would still be weak.

cards.q: Which enzyme generates cyclic AMP?
cards.a: Adenylyl cyclase.
options: Phospholipase C
Adenylyl cyclase
Phosphodiesterase
Protein kinase A
cards.explanation: Adenylyl cyclase sits in the plasma membrane and converts ATP into cyclic AMP once a Gs protein activates it. Phospholipase C generates IP3 and diacylglycerol instead. Phosphodiesterase breaks cyclic AMP down, and protein kinase A is the enzyme cyclic AMP activates rather than the one that makes it.

cards.q: What is the main target activated by cyclic AMP?
cards.a: Protein kinase A.
options: Calmodulin
Protein kinase C
Protein kinase A
Phospholipase C
cards.explanation: Cyclic AMP binds the regulatory subunits of protein kinase A and releases the catalytic subunits, which then phosphorylate a long list of cellular proteins. Protein kinase C is activated by diacylglycerol and calcium. Calmodulin is the calcium binding partner, and phospholipase C is an amplifier enzyme in the other branch of the pathway.

cards.q: Which enzyme generates both IP3 and diacylglycerol?
cards.a: Phospholipase C.
options: Adenylyl cyclase
Guanylyl cyclase
Protein kinase C
Phospholipase C
cards.explanation: Phospholipase C cleaves the membrane phospholipid PIP2, and the single cut yields both messengers at once. Adenylyl cyclase and guanylyl cyclase make the cyclic nucleotides cyclic AMP and cyclic GMP. Protein kinase C is a downstream target of diacylglycerol, so it is a consumer of the signal rather than its source.

cards.q: What does IP3 do once it is released into the cytosol?
cards.a: Opens calcium release channels on the endoplasmic reticulum.
options: Opens calcium release channels on the endoplasmic reticulum
Activates protein kinase A directly
Opens sodium channels in the plasma membrane and depolarizes it
Binds DNA and starts transcription
cards.explanation: IP3 is water soluble, so it diffuses off the membrane and binds receptors on the endoplasmic reticulum that release stored calcium into the cytosol. Protein kinase A is activated by cyclic AMP, not by IP3. IP3 does not gate plasma membrane sodium channels, and it is not a transcription factor, since its effects are immediate rather than gene mediated.

cards.q: Which second messenger stays in the plasma membrane and activates protein kinase C?
cards.a: Diacylglycerol.
options: IP3
Diacylglycerol
Calcium
Cyclic AMP
cards.explanation: Diacylglycerol keeps its fatty acid tails after PIP2 is cleaved, so it stays in the bilayer and recruits protein kinase C to the membrane. IP3 is the water soluble half of that same cleavage and leaves for the cytosol. Cyclic AMP is a soluble nucleotide, and calcium is an ion that moves freely in the cytosol rather than remaining in the membrane.

cards.q: Calcium acting as a second messenger commonly works by binding which regulatory protein?
cards.a: Calmodulin.
options: Phospholipase C
Adenylyl cyclase
Calmodulin
Protein kinase A
cards.explanation: Calcium binds calmodulin, and the calcium calmodulin complex then activates a family of kinases and other enzymes, which is how the ion is converted into a protein signal. Adenylyl cyclase and phospholipase C are amplifier enzymes upstream of second messengers. Protein kinase A is activated by cyclic AMP, not by calcium binding.

cards.q: What is a second messenger?
cards.a: An intracellular molecule made in response to a signal, which relays the message inside the cell.
options: A hormone that acts on a second target tissue after the first one has responded
A protein secreted by the target cell that amplifies the original signal it received from outside
A receptor that binds a ligand after the first receptor is saturated with ligand
An intracellular molecule made in response to a signal, which relays the message inside the cell
cards.explanation: The first messenger is the extracellular ligand and the second messenger is the internal molecule, such as cyclic AMP or calcium, that carries the message onward from the membrane. A hormone acting on a second tissue is still a first messenger. A backup receptor is not a messenger, and a secreted protein leaves the cell rather than relaying a signal inside it.

cards.q: Where is the calcium that IP3 releases stored inside the cell?
cards.a: In the endoplasmic reticulum.
options: In the endoplasmic reticulum
In the Golgi vesicles awaiting export
In the nucleus
Dissolved freely in the cytosol
cards.explanation: The endoplasmic reticulum, called the sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle, pumps calcium in and holds it at high concentration so it can be dumped into the cytosol on command. The nucleus and Golgi are not the calcium reservoirs used for signaling. Free cytosolic calcium is deliberately kept very low at rest, which is exactly what makes a sudden release detectable.

cards.q: Resting cytosolic calcium is about 0.0001 mM while extracellular calcium is about 1 mM. Why does the cell hold the cytosolic level so low?
cards.a: So that a small release or influx produces a large fractional change the cell can read as a signal.
options: So that calcium cannot bind calmodulin while the cell is at rest, which would waste ATP needlessly
So that a small release or influx produces a large fractional change the cell can read as a signal
So that calcium can serve as the main source of energy for the cell's work
So that the resting membrane potential of the cell stays strongly negative
cards.explanation: A signal has to stand out from background, and starting near zero means opening a channel for a fraction of a second can raise cytosolic calcium ten fold or more. Preventing calmodulin binding at rest is a consequence of the low level, not the design reason, and the pumping does cost ATP. Calcium is not an energy source, and the resting potential is set mainly by potassium permeability.

cards.q: A drug mimics diacylglycerol at its binding site. Which enzyme would you expect to become active?
cards.a: Protein kinase C.
options: Protein kinase A
Adenylyl cyclase
Protein kinase C
Phosphodiesterase
cards.explanation: Diacylglycerol recruits and activates protein kinase C at the membrane, so a mimic occupies that same site and switches the kinase on without any ligand at the receptor. Protein kinase A responds to cyclic AMP, a different messenger. Adenylyl cyclase is activated by Gs, and phosphodiesterase is a degrading enzyme rather than a diacylglycerol target.

cards.q: A drug blocks the IP3 receptor on the endoplasmic reticulum. A Gq agonist is then applied. Predict what happens to cytosolic calcium.
cards.a: It fails to rise from internal stores, even though IP3 is still made.
options: It rises normally, because IP3 also opens plasma membrane calcium channels
It rises more than normal, because the blocked receptor cannot close
It falls below resting level, because the stores keep pumping calcium in
It fails to rise from internal stores, even though IP3 is still made
cards.explanation: Phospholipase C still cleaves PIP2 and IP3 still accumulates, but with its receptor blocked the messenger has nothing to open, so the store stays loaded. The classic IP3 action is on the endoplasmic reticulum rather than on the plasma membrane. Resting calcium is already low and continued pumping produces no dramatic further fall, and a blocked receptor cannot conduct calcium at all.

cards.q: You measure a rise in cyclic AMP in a cell. Which downstream activity should rise if the pathway is intact?
cards.a: Phosphorylation of proteins by protein kinase A.
options: Phosphorylation of proteins by protein kinase A
Cleavage of PIP2 by phospholipase C
Release of calcium through IP3 receptors
Transcription driven by a steroid receptor
cards.explanation: Cyclic AMP has one main job, activating protein kinase A, so its rise should be followed by increased phosphorylation of that kinase's substrates. PIP2 cleavage and IP3 mediated calcium release belong to the Gq branch and are not triggered by cyclic AMP. Steroid receptor transcription requires a lipophilic hormone and an intracellular receptor, not a second messenger.

cards.q: Calcium calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase in vascular smooth muscle. Predict the effect of a Gq agonist on that muscle.
cards.a: It contracts, because IP3 raises calcium and the kinase is activated.
options: It relaxes, because calcium inhibits the kinase
It contracts, because IP3 raises calcium and the kinase is activated
It is unaffected, because smooth muscle lacks calmodulin
It contracts only after several hours of new protein synthesis
cards.explanation: The Gq agonist generates IP3, calcium leaves the stores, calcium calmodulin turns on myosin light chain kinase, and phosphorylated myosin cross bridges cycle. Calcium activates rather than inhibits this kinase, which is why raising it causes contraction. Smooth muscle relies on calmodulin because it lacks troponin, and the whole sequence uses existing proteins, so it takes seconds rather than hours.

cards.q: A cell is loaded with a chelator that buffers cytosolic calcium to a very low level. A Gq agonist is applied. Which part of the response is lost?
cards.a: Every step that depends on the calcium rise, while IP3 and diacylglycerol are still produced.
options: Ligand binding at the receptor, since binding to the surface receptor itself requires calcium
Production of IP3, since IP3 synthesis by phospholipase C requires calcium
Every step that depends on the calcium rise, while IP3 and diacylglycerol are still produced
Nothing at all, since calcium acts as a messenger only in muscle cells
cards.explanation: A chelator sits downstream of messenger production, so phospholipase C still cleaves PIP2 while any calcium that is released is captured before it can act. IP3 synthesis is driven by the G protein and does not require cytosolic calcium. Ligand binding is a surface event independent of internal calcium, and calcium serves as a second messenger in almost every cell type, not only muscle.

cards.q: Which pairing of messenger, generating enzyme, and target is correct?
cards.a: IP3, phospholipase C, endoplasmic reticulum calcium release channel.
options: Cyclic AMP, phospholipase C, protein kinase C in the plasma membrane
Calcium, adenylyl cyclase, protein kinase A
Diacylglycerol, adenylyl cyclase, calmodulin
IP3, phospholipase C, endoplasmic reticulum calcium release channel
cards.explanation: Phospholipase C makes IP3, and IP3 opens the release channel that lets stored calcium into the cytosol, so all three parts belong together. Cyclic AMP comes from adenylyl cyclase and acts on protein kinase A. Diacylglycerol comes from phospholipase C and acts on protein kinase C, and calcium is released from stores or enters through channels rather than being made by a cyclase.

cards.q: A Gq agonist is applied to a cell whose IP3 receptors are blocked. Predict the effect on protein kinase C activity compared with a normal cell.
cards.a: Partial activation, because diacylglycerol is still made but the helping calcium rise is missing.
options: Partial activation, because diacylglycerol is still made but the helping calcium rise is missing
Full activation, because diacylglycerol alone is sufficient and is not affected here
No activation, because diacylglycerol cannot be made without IP3 receptor binding
Greater than normal activation, because unused IP3 accumulates and activates the kinase
cards.explanation: Cleaving PIP2 produces both messengers, so diacylglycerol is unaffected by an IP3 receptor block, but conventional protein kinase C is activated best by diacylglycerol together with calcium, so the response is blunted. Diacylglycerol production depends on phospholipase C, not on the IP3 receptor. Accumulated IP3 has no action once its receptor is blocked, so it cannot boost the kinase.

cards.q: Epinephrine binds a beta receptor on a liver cell. Trace the second messenger pathway to the effect on blood glucose.
cards.a: Cyclic AMP rises, protein kinase A is activated, glycogen breakdown increases, and glucose is released into the blood.
options: IP3 rises, calcium is released, glycogen synthesis increases, and blood glucose falls
Cyclic AMP rises, protein kinase A is activated, glycogen breakdown increases, and glucose is released into the blood
Cyclic AMP falls, protein kinase A is inhibited, and the liver stores more glucose
Diacylglycerol rises, protein kinase C is activated, and the liver takes up glucose from the circulating blood
cards.explanation: Beta receptors couple to Gs, and the cyclic AMP that follows activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates the enzymes of glycogen metabolism so breakdown is favored and glucose leaves the liver. An answer built on IP3 and increased glycogen synthesis runs the pathway backward and names the wrong messenger. Falling cyclic AMP is a Gi response, and the diacylglycerol version assigns the wrong messenger and the wrong direction of glucose movement.

cards.q: IP3 and diacylglycerol are produced at the same instant from the same lipid, yet they act at different places in the cell. What accounts for the difference and what does each reach?
cards.a: IP3 is water soluble and diffuses through the cytosol to the endoplasmic reticulum, while diacylglycerol stays in the membrane.
options: Both stay in the membrane, but IP3 is degraded faster, so it acts for a shorter time near its source
IP3 is lipid soluble and stays in the membrane, while diacylglycerol dissolves in the cytosol and reaches the nucleus
IP3 is water soluble and diffuses through the cytosol to the endoplasmic reticulum, while diacylglycerol stays in the membrane
Both diffuse through the cytosol, but diacylglycerol is larger and therefore moves more slowly
cards.explanation: Solubility decides destination: stripping the phosphorylated head group off PIP2 releases a polar molecule into the cytosol while leaving the fatty tails behind in the bilayer. Reversing their solubilities reverses their destinations and is the common misconception here. Diacylglycerol does not travel through cytosol at all, so explanations based only on degradation speed or molecular size miss the mechanism.

cards.q: A cell is bathed in calcium free solution and given a Gq agonist. Cytosolic calcium spikes briefly, then returns to baseline and stays there despite continued agonist. Explain both observations.
cards.a: The spike came from internal stores, and without extracellular calcium those stores cannot be refilled.
options: The calcium pumps failed, so calcium leaked back out of the cell permanently
The spike came from the extracellular fluid, and the small residual amount was quickly used up
IP3 production stopped after a few seconds, even though PIP2 is unlimited
The spike came from internal stores, and without extracellular calcium those stores cannot be refilled
cards.explanation: IP3 empties the endoplasmic reticulum first, which explains the initial spike even with no calcium outside, and sustained signaling normally depends on entry across the plasma membrane to keep the stores loaded. The extracellular fluid was calcium free, so it cannot be the source of the spike. Saying PIP2 is unlimited contradicts the claim that IP3 production stopped, and failing pumps would raise rather than lower cytosolic calcium.

cards.q: The insulin receptor belongs to which class of receptor?
cards.a: A receptor enzyme with tyrosine kinase activity.
options: A receptor enzyme with tyrosine kinase activity
A G protein coupled receptor
A ligand gated ion channel
A nuclear transcription factor receptor
cards.explanation: The insulin receptor spans the membrane and its cytosolic portion is itself an enzyme, a tyrosine kinase, so binding insulin switches on catalytic activity directly with no G protein in between. A G protein coupled receptor would need a separate amplifier enzyme. Ligand gated channels conduct ions rather than phosphorylate proteins, and a nuclear receptor would require insulin to enter the cell, which a peptide cannot do.

cards.q: What chemical change does a tyrosine kinase make to its target proteins?
cards.a: It adds a phosphate group to tyrosine residues.
options: It removes a phosphate group from tyrosine residues
It adds a phosphate group to tyrosine residues
It cleaves the protein at tyrosine residues
It adds a methyl group to tyrosine residues
cards.explanation: Kinases transfer a phosphate from ATP onto a specific amino acid, and adding that bulky negative charge changes the target protein's shape and activity. Removing phosphate is the job of a phosphatase, which is how these signals are reversed. Cleaving the protein is proteolysis, and methylation is a different modification used mainly in gene regulation.

cards.q: Where is the receptor for a steroid hormone such as cortisol located?
cards.a: In the cytosol or nucleus of the target cell.
options: On the outer surface of the plasma membrane
In the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum
In the cytosol or nucleus of the target cell
On the surface of circulating carrier proteins
cards.explanation: Cortisol crosses the membrane on its own, so its receptor waits inside the cell and the hormone receptor complex then acts on DNA. A plasma membrane receptor is needed only by signals that cannot cross. The endoplasmic reticulum lumen is not a signaling compartment for steroids, and carrier proteins transport hormone in blood without transmitting a message.

cards.q: What is the immediate product of intracellular steroid receptor activation?
cards.a: Changed transcription of specific genes.
options: A rise in cyclic AMP
Opening of a calcium release channel
Phosphorylation of tyrosine residues
Changed transcription of specific genes
cards.explanation: The activated complex binds regulatory DNA and turns particular genes up or down, so its output is messenger RNA and then protein. Cyclic AMP and calcium release belong to membrane receptor pathways with second messengers. Tyrosine phosphorylation is the mechanism of a receptor enzyme like the insulin receptor, not of a nuclear receptor.

cards.q: Which produces a measurable cellular response sooner, insulin acting on its receptor or cortisol acting on its receptor?
cards.a: Insulin, within minutes.
options: Insulin, within minutes
Cortisol, within seconds
Both act within milliseconds
Cortisol, because it does not need a receptor
cards.explanation: Insulin activates a kinase that modifies proteins the cell already has, so glucose uptake rises within minutes. Cortisol must change gene expression and wait for protein synthesis, which takes tens of minutes to hours. Neither is a millisecond event, since that speed belongs to ligand gated ion channels, and cortisol certainly does require a receptor.

cards.q: What is autophosphorylation in a receptor enzyme?
cards.a: The receptor adds phosphate groups to its own cytosolic portion after ligand binds.
options: The receptor is phosphorylated by a separate kinase before ligand binds
The receptor adds phosphate groups to its own cytosolic portion after ligand binds
The receptor removes its own phosphate groups to become active
The receptor transfers a phosphate to the ligand it just bound
cards.explanation: When ligand binding brings two receptor halves together, each kinase domain phosphorylates the other, and those new phosphotyrosines become docking sites for signaling proteins. Phosphorylation by an outside kinase is a different regulatory event and is not what the prefix auto describes. Removing phosphate is dephosphorylation, and the ligand itself is not the phosphate acceptor.

cards.q: In muscle and fat cells, insulin receptor signaling increases glucose uptake mainly by doing what?
cards.a: Moving GLUT4 transporters into the plasma membrane.
options: Opening voltage gated glucose channels
Increasing transcription of the glucose transporter gene over several hours
Moving GLUT4 transporters into the plasma membrane
Pumping glucose in against its gradient using ATP
cards.explanation: Vesicles holding GLUT4 are already sitting in the cytosol, so inserting them into the membrane raises glucose permeability within minutes and requires no new protein. There is no voltage gated glucose channel, since glucose crosses by carrier mediated transport. Transcription would take hours and would not match insulin's speed, and GLUT4 carries glucose down its gradient without using ATP.

cards.q: What is the name of the DNA sequence that an activated steroid receptor complex binds?
cards.a: A hormone response element.
options: A second messenger promoter
A ligand binding domain
A synaptic cleft consensus site
A hormone response element
cards.explanation: A hormone response element is the short regulatory DNA sequence near a target gene where the hormone receptor complex docks to change transcription. The ligand binding domain is a part of the receptor protein, not a piece of DNA. The other two options are invented terms that mix vocabulary from unrelated parts of the pathway.

cards.q: A hormone increases an enzyme's activity within 5 minutes, and the effect survives treatment with a protein synthesis inhibitor. Which receptor type is it using?
cards.a: A receptor enzyme in the plasma membrane.
options: A receptor enzyme in the plasma membrane
A cytosolic steroid receptor
A nuclear thyroid hormone receptor
A receptor bound to a hormone response element
cards.explanation: Speed plus independence from the ribosome means the hormone is modifying proteins that already exist, which is what a membrane bound receptor kinase does. All three other options are transcription linked receptors whose effects appear slowly and vanish when protein synthesis is blocked. Those receptors would fit a response measured over hours instead.

cards.q: A mutation removes the kinase activity of the insulin receptor but leaves the insulin binding site intact. Predict the results of a binding assay and of a glucose uptake assay.
cards.a: Insulin binding is normal and glucose uptake fails to increase.
options: Both binding and glucose uptake are normal
Insulin binding is normal and glucose uptake fails to increase
Insulin binding fails and glucose uptake increases normally anyway
Both binding and glucose uptake fail
cards.explanation: Binding and signaling are separate functions of the same protein, so an intact extracellular site still captures insulin while the dead kinase cannot start the cascade that moves GLUT4. Normal uptake would require the kinase, which is exactly what is missing. Binding failure would require damage to the extracellular domain, which the mutation spared.

cards.q: Cells are treated with a transcription inhibitor. Cortisol's effect disappears but insulin's effect on glucose uptake remains. Why?
cards.a: Cortisol works only by making new proteins, while insulin modifies transporters the cell already has.
options: Insulin is a steroid hormone and is therefore resistant to any inhibitor of gene transcription
Cortisol binds a surface receptor that the inhibitor happens to block as well
Cortisol works only by making new proteins, while insulin modifies transporters the cell already has
Insulin reaches the nucleus faster than cortisol does in these cultured cells
cards.explanation: The experiment separates the two mechanisms cleanly: a gene mediated response depends on transcription and a kinase mediated response does not. Cortisol uses an intracellular receptor rather than a surface receptor. Insulin is a peptide, not a steroid, and it never enters the nucleus, since its receptor works from the plasma membrane.

cards.q: Both hormones are washed out of a culture after a brief exposure. Which effect is more likely to persist for hours and why?
cards.a: The steroid effect, because the proteins it induced remain until they are degraded.
options: The insulin effect, because phosphate groups are permanent
Both equally, because washing removes only free hormone
Neither effect, because both depend on the continuous presence of their hormone
The steroid effect, because the proteins it induced remain until they are degraded
cards.explanation: Gene mediated responses leave behind physical protein molecules with lifetimes of hours to days, so the effect outlasts the hormone. Phosphate groups are quickly removed by phosphatases, so kinase driven effects reverse within minutes. Persistence after washout is exactly what distinguishes the two hormones, so answers claiming that neither effect persists or that both persist equally miss the difference in mechanism.

cards.q: A receptor has its ligand binding site facing the extracellular fluid and a catalytic domain projecting into the cytosol. How should it be classified?
cards.a: A receptor enzyme.
options: A receptor enzyme
An intracellular receptor
A G protein coupled receptor
A ligand gated ion channel
cards.explanation: A single protein that both binds ligand outside and catalyzes a reaction inside is the definition of a receptor enzyme, the family that includes the insulin receptor. An intracellular receptor would have no extracellular domain at all. A G protein coupled receptor has no catalytic domain of its own, and an ion channel forms a conducting pore rather than a catalytic site.

cards.q: A mutation damages the DNA binding domain of a receptor. Which hormone's signaling would be impaired?
cards.a: Cortisol.
options: Insulin
Cortisol
Epinephrine
Acetylcholine
cards.explanation: Only receptors that act as transcription factors have a DNA binding domain, so a steroid such as cortisol is the one that loses its pathway. Insulin acts through a membrane kinase and epinephrine through a G protein, neither of which touches DNA directly. Acetylcholine works through ion channels or G protein coupled receptors, also without a DNA binding step.

cards.q: A steroid receptor mutation leaves ligand binding intact but prevents the complex from entering the nucleus. Predict what a researcher would find for hormone uptake into the cell, receptor binding, and messenger RNA levels.
cards.a: Uptake normal, binding normal, and no change in messenger RNA.
options: Uptake reduced, binding reduced, and no change in messenger RNA
Uptake normal, binding absent, and messenger RNA increased
Uptake normal, binding normal, and no change in messenger RNA
Uptake normal, binding normal, and messenger RNA increased as usual
cards.explanation: The hormone still crosses the membrane by lipid solubility and still binds its receptor, but a complex stuck in the cytosol never reaches the DNA, so transcription is unchanged. Uptake does not depend on the receptor, so reduced uptake does not follow. Binding was explicitly preserved, and a normal messenger RNA rise would require the nuclear step that the mutation blocks.

cards.q: After a meal, insulin lowers blood glucose within minutes. Cortisol raises blood glucose over hours by increasing the enzymes of gluconeogenesis. What accounts for the difference in time course?
cards.a: Insulin modifies existing transporters and enzymes, while cortisol must produce new enzyme molecules.
options: Insulin is far more potent per molecule than cortisol is when the two act on the same tissue
Insulin circulates through the blood faster than cortisol does after a meal
Cortisol must first be converted into a peptide before it can act on the cell
Insulin modifies existing transporters and enzymes, while cortisol must produce new enzyme molecules
cards.explanation: Time course follows mechanism: phosphorylation and vesicle insertion are fast because the machinery is already built, while transcription and translation take time to accumulate enough enzyme to matter. Potency describes how much hormone is needed, not how quickly it works. Cortisol is not converted to a peptide, and both hormones reach tissues in the same circulation within seconds.

cards.q: A cell is exposed to cortisol for several hours and then given epinephrine. The cyclic AMP response to epinephrine is larger than in an untreated cell. What is the most likely explanation?
cards.a: Cortisol increased transcription of beta receptors, so more receptors were present for epinephrine.
options: Cortisol increased transcription of beta receptors, so more receptors were present for epinephrine
Cortisol bound the beta receptor directly and added its own signal to that of epinephrine
Cortisol inhibited adenylyl cyclase, which made the later response rebound higher
Cortisol converted the beta receptor into a nuclear receptor during those hours
cards.explanation: A gene mediated hormone can change how a cell responds to a later signal by altering how many receptors or downstream proteins it expresses, and the hours long delay fits transcription. Cortisol does not bind adrenergic receptors, so it cannot add a direct signal. Inhibiting the cyclase would blunt rather than amplify the response, and receptors are not converted from one class to another.

cards.q: A phosphatase inhibitor is added to cells stimulated with insulin. Predict what happens to the insulin response after the hormone is washed away, and explain why.
cards.a: The response persists longer than normal, because the phosphates placed by the receptor kinase are not removed.
options: The response ends sooner, because phosphatases are needed to sustain signaling
The response persists longer than normal, because the phosphates placed by the receptor kinase are not removed
The response is unchanged, because washing removes the receptor along with the hormone
The response becomes gene mediated, because prolonged signaling recruits nuclear receptors to the pathway
cards.explanation: Kinase driven signals are normally brief because phosphatases strip the phosphate groups off within minutes, so blocking that removal leaves target proteins phosphorylated and active after the hormone is gone. Phosphatases terminate rather than sustain the signal. Washing removes free hormone but leaves receptors in the membrane, and a receptor enzyme does not turn into a nuclear receptor.

cards.q: What does signal amplification mean in a cell signaling pathway?
cards.a: One bound ligand molecule leads to a much larger number of product or response molecules.
options: The receptor increases its affinity for the ligand as the signal continues
The ligand concentration in the blood rises during the response
One bound ligand molecule leads to a much larger number of product or response molecules
The response spreads from one cell to neighboring cells through gap junctions
cards.explanation: Amplification is a numerical idea: each step multiplies the number of active molecules, so a single binding event ends in thousands or millions of product molecules. Rising ligand concentration in blood is a change in the input, not amplification inside the cell. Increased affinity would change binding rather than multiply output, and spread between cells is a separate phenomenon from cascade gain.

cards.q: In a G protein coupled receptor pathway, where does amplification begin?
cards.a: One activated receptor activates many G protein molecules.
options: One ligand binds many receptors at once
One second messenger molecule binds many receptors at the surface
One G protein binds many ligands
One activated receptor activates many G protein molecules
cards.explanation: A single occupied receptor can cycle through and switch on many G proteins before the ligand leaves, so the first multiplication happens right at the membrane. A single ligand molecule occupies one receptor at a time, so binding itself does not amplify. G proteins do not bind ligand, and second messengers act downstream on kinases rather than back on receptors.

cards.q: Why does one activated adenylyl cyclase molecule amplify the signal?
cards.a: Because it is an enzyme and converts many ATP molecules into cyclic AMP while it stays active.
options: Because it is an enzyme and converts many ATP molecules into cyclic AMP while it stays active
Because it binds many G proteins at once and adds their signals together
Because it is consumed in the reaction, releasing all of the signal molecules it had stored
Because it doubles in number every time a G protein activates it again
cards.explanation: Catalysis is the source of gain, since an enzyme is not used up and keeps turning over substrate for as long as it remains active. Binding many G proteins at once is not how the cyclase works, and one activating G protein is enough. Enzymes are not consumed in their reactions, and they do not replicate themselves during signaling.

cards.q: Which feature of a cascade makes it capable of large amplification?
cards.a: Each active enzyme acts catalytically on many substrate molecules.
options: Each step uses a different second messenger
Each active enzyme acts catalytically on many substrate molecules
Each step is reversible, so signal can flow both directions
Each step requires a new receptor to be synthesized
cards.explanation: Turnover number is the engine of amplification: one enzyme molecule handles many substrate molecules per second, and stacking such steps multiplies the gain. Using different messengers adds versatility but not gain by itself. Cascades flow in one direction under normal conditions, and no step waits for new receptor synthesis, which would slow rather than amplify the signal.

cards.q: Which step in a signaling pathway does not amplify the signal?
cards.a: A ligand binding to one receptor.
options: An enzyme generating second messenger molecules
A kinase phosphorylating many target proteins
A ligand binding to one receptor
A G protein activating an amplifier enzyme that then works repeatedly
cards.explanation: Binding is a one to one event, so it converts a single ligand into a single occupied receptor with no multiplication. Enzymes making messengers and kinases phosphorylating many targets are both catalytic steps with high gain. A G protein activating an enzyme that then turns over substrate repeatedly also multiplies, because the gain comes from the enzyme it switches on.

cards.q: When a pathway has several amplifying steps in series, how do their individual gains combine?
cards.a: They multiply.
options: They add
Only the largest one counts
They average
They multiply
cards.explanation: Each step takes the output of the step before it as its input, so gains compound and three modest steps can produce a very large final number. Adding them would badly underestimate the output. Averaging is not how sequential processes combine, and every step contributes, which is why a single step with no gain can hold the whole pathway back.
